subject: biology
title: The nitrogen cycle
key_idea: Plants need **nitrates** from the soil to make proteins. Bacteria move nitrogen between the air, the soil and living things. Farmers add nitrates with fertilisers, manure and crop rotation.

blocks.text: Plants cannot use nitrogen gas from the air. They take in nitrate ions from the soil through their roots.

items: Nitrates are used to make proteins (from amino acids) and chlorophyll.
Proteins are needed for growth, so more nitrate in the soil improves crop yield.
A low nitrate concentration in the soil gives poor plant growth.
Plants take up nitrates from the soil.
Nitrates are used to make proteins, which are needed for growth.

blocks.text: Four groups of microorganisms keep nitrogen cycling between the air, the soil and living things.

items.meaning: Bacteria and fungi that break down waste matter and dead organisms, releasing ammonia.
Bacteria that convert ammonia into nitrites and then nitrates.
Bacteria that convert nitrogen gas from the air into nitrates or ammonia.
Bacteria that convert nitrates back into nitrogen gas.

items: Some nitrogen-fixing bacteria live in colonies in **root nodules** on peas and beans. This is a mutualistic relationship.
Other nitrogen-fixing bacteria live in the soil.
Plants take up the nitrates. Animals get nitrogen compounds by eating plants or other animals.

blocks.text: Crops remove nitrates from the soil as they grow. Farmers and gardeners replace them in several ways.

rows: Add nitrate compounds directly to the soil
Manure, slurry, green manure and compost
Decomposers break down the waste and dead plant matter, so minerals and nitrogen compounds return to the soil
Turns some nitrogen gas in the air into compounds that dissolve in rain and reach the soil as nitrates
A leguminous crop such as peas or beans is grown in some years. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria in its root nodules fix nitrogen gas from the air
Nitrogen-fixing and nitrifying bacteria make nitrates naturally

blocks.text: Crop rotation reduces the need to add nitrate fertilisers. Excess fertiliser can be washed into lakes and rivers, where it causes eutrophication.

items: Fertilisers, manure, compost and crop rotation all increase nitrates in the soil.
Leguminous crops have nitrogen-fixing bacteria in root nodules, so rotation reduces the need for fertilisers.

blocks.text: (Supplement) Follow the nitrogen through the whole cycle, in living things as well as in the soil.

items: **Decomposition:** decomposers break down plant and animal protein and release ammonium ions.
**Nitrification:** nitrifying bacteria convert ammonium ions into nitrate ions.
**Absorption:** plants take in nitrate ions and use them to make amino acids, then proteins.
**Feeding and digestion:** animals eat the protein and digest it to amino acids.
**Deamination:** the liver removes the nitrogen part of excess amino acids and makes urea, which is excreted.
**Nitrogen fixation:** lightning and nitrogen-fixing bacteria turn nitrogen gas into nitrogen compounds.
**Denitrification:** denitrifying bacteria turn nitrates back into nitrogen gas.

worked_example.question:
A student investigates the nitrogen cycle. She takes two samples of soil, each of mass 100 g. She sterilises one sample by heating it at 100 °C for one hour. She washes both samples with water until no nitrates are found. She then adds 1 cm³ of a solution of ammonium salts to each soil and leaves them for three days. She then tests water poured through each soil for nitrates.

Three days after adding the ammonium salts, nitrates are present in the unsterilised soil and absent in the sterilised soil.

Comment on these results.
answer_points: Nitrates are present in the unsterilised soil.
The nitrates were made from the ammonium salts.
Nitrifying bacteria (nitrification) converted ammonium into nitrite, then nitrite into nitrate.
There are no nitrates in the sterilised soil because the bacteria were killed.
The test was not repeated and did not measure the quantity of nitrates.
worked_example.tip: Any four of these score one mark each.
